You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Leilani Makana was sixty-six years old, a divorced shopowner of Pacific Islander descent who had run a small convenience store in her neighborhood for thirty years. The event that shattered her sense of safety happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just after she had locked up for the night. Two plainclothes officers approached her in the alley behind the store, shouting questions she could not understand, their flashlights blinding her. She remembered raising her hands, the cold metal of a gun pressed against her temple, the gravel scraping her knees as she was forced to the ground. The rest was a blur of pain, shouting, and the smell of asphalt. She had come to believe there were parts of that night she simply could not recall, no matter how hard she tried—gaps that felt like holes in her own history. The memory itself was so extreme that it hardly seemed real; sometimes she sat and stared at her hands and wondered if any of it had actually happened, or if she had dreamed the whole thing. But she could not put it into words. When her daughter asked what occurred, Leilani’s mouth went dry; she shook her head and said, “I can’t tell it.” The story felt trapped somewhere in her body, not in her mind.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani noticed that the time of day the event had happened—just after dusk, when the alley behind the store grew dark—became unbearable. As the sun dipped below the roofline, her chest tightened and her vision dimmed. She began closing the shop an hour earlier, telling herself it was better for business to adjust, but the real reason was that she could not bear being outside after that hour. She also started avoiding any place that was dimly lit; at home she kept every lamp on, even in the daytime, because the shadows reminded her of the flashlights and the sudden sensation of being watched. The feeling of being observed was constant now. In the store, she would glance over her shoulder at customers, certain they were studying her, waiting for her to slip up. Even the security camera above the register felt accusatory. When she felt dizzy—a sensation that came without warning, a lightheaded spin that made her grab the counter—she was sure she was about to collapse, that her body was betraying her, that her reactions since the event proved she was a lousy coper. She began to fear that she was going crazy, that her mind was finally breaking after all these years of running the shop alone.

To manage the constant dread, Leilani developed habits that she knew, somewhere beneath the panic, were not helping. She avoided any mention of the date the event had occurred; when October came around the next year, she threw away the calendar page and refused to open her mail. But the avoidance took a different form as well: she spent money. At first it was small things—a candle, a new teapot—but soon she was buying clothes she never wore, gadgets she did not need, online orders arriving daily at the shop. It was a way to feel something other than fear, a few minutes of focus on the screen instead of on the watching eyes she imagined behind her. She knew the credit card bills were piling up, but the thought of stopping made the dizziness surge, and she would click “buy” again to push it away.

The consequence of her avoidance was tangible. Her shop, once a lively hub where neighbors stopped to chat, grew quiet. Leilani rushed customers through their purchases, kept the blinds half-drawn, and stopped stocking the shelves herself because she refused to walk into the back storage room where the light switch clicked with a sound that reminded her of a gun's safety. Her daughter, who had once helped on weekends, stopped coming because Leilani snapped at her when she tried to talk about what happened. The relationship grew brittle, another loss layered onto the trauma.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a morning in late spring when she woke up and could not remember how she had gotten home from the shop the night before. The gap in memory was terrifying, tipping her into the old fear that she was truly losing her mind. She made an appointment at a clinic downtown, not because she hoped to feel better, but because she was afraid of what might happen if she did not. She sat in the waiting room with her hands clasped, her eyes fixed on a clock whose hands were moving inexorably toward the time of day she dreaded most. She was not sure what she wanted—perhaps just for someone to tell her that she was not crazy, that the gaps and the dizziness and the spending were all part of something she could name. But even that felt too much to hope for.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Inadequacy: The vignette does not mention or illustrate the patient's feeling of being inadequate; it only covers 'bad coper' and 'fear going crazy'.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

She felt fundamentally unequal to the demands of her own life: inadequate as a shopkeeper who could no longer keep her business running the way it always had, inadequate as a mother who could not find the words to explain to her daughter why she was so changed, and inadequate as a person who could not simply snap out of it. The purchases were also a fragile antidote to the inadequacy; for a brief moment, holding a new object in her hands, she felt like someone who could still make choices, who still had control.

Leilani rushed customers through their purchases, kept the blinds half-drawn, and stopped stocking the shelves herself because she refused to walk into the back storage room where the light switch clicked with a sound that reminded her of a gun's safety. Her daughter, who had once helped on weekends, stopped coming because Leilani snapped at her when she tried to talk about what happened. The relationship grew brittle, another loss layered onto the trauma, and it only deepened Leilani’s conviction that she was inadequate—unable even to hold on to the people she loved.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a morning in late spring when she woke up and could not remember how she had gotten home from the shop the night before. The gap in memory was terrifying, tipping her into the old fear that she was truly losing her mind. She made an appointment at a clinic downtown, not because she hoped to feel better, but because she was afraid of what might happen if she did not. She sat in the waiting room with her hands clasped, her eyes fixed on a clock whose hands were moving inexorably toward the time of day she dreaded most. She was not sure what she wanted—perhaps just for someone to tell her that she was not crazy, that the gaps and the dizziness and the spending and the awful feeling of inadequacy were all part of something she could name.
